en: Under patch 25.24, Riot records the release of prestige cosmetic content with a precise date: “Prestige Winterblessed Mel will be available December 3, 2025.” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025e)</2>. The record proves the existence of an institutional offer window tied to rarity and recognition, relevant to characterizing the ecosystem's symbolic economy and its articulation with attention cycles. <3>↩</3>

In patch 26.3, Riot describes the defensive change as a “big change”, recording: “A big change we have is changing your immunity to reflected damage into a shield […]” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026d)</2>. The passage is useful because it shows that this is not a merely incremental adjustment, but a decision aimed at reconfiguring the patterns of interaction and counterplay deemed acceptable by the system. <3>↩</3>

In the same patch, the modification appears objectively formalized in the ability description: “No longer grants damage immunity.” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026d)</2>. The information suffices to show that there was a qualitative change to the mechanism, with the potential to alter the very practical expectation of enjoyment and in the functional stability of the acquired asset. <3>↩</3>

“The grand object therefore of the modern manufacturer is, through the union of capital and science, to reduce the task of his work-people to the exercise of vigilance and dexterity.” <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 54)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Feenberg makes explicit that the “technical code” may stabilize divergent solutions according to the balance of forces among social interests. “The technical code would in the one case impose skilled work and in the other deskilling, reflecting the different interests of workers and managers.” <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2002, p. 91)</2>. The author maintains that the act of “optimizing” cannot be understood as a neutral operation, since it implies choosing which interest will be translated into technical coherence. In digital ecosystems, the analogy shifts to the interface. Design may expand the user's capacities (control, audit, reversibility) or may restrict them in the name of organizational predictability, always in the idiom of the functional “best solution”. <3>↩</3>

“The deskilling of manual labor and its total submission to management foreshadows the spread of similarly authoritarian relations between administrators and their employees/clients in technologically advanced societies during the twentieth century.” <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 55)</2>. <3>↩</3>

In formulating the notion of “operational autonomy”, Feenberg <1>(2002, p. 43)</1> seeks to show that capitalist control of the productive process is not exercised only through legal-formal command or administrative coordination, but is consolidated when the organization of work itself is technically incorporated. It is at this point that the author turns to Karl Marx (citing an edition of <2>Capital</2> published in 1906) to maintain that the specifically capitalist form of organizing the labor process acquires a palpable technical reality insofar as machinery and productive arrangements transform the worker into a subordinate component of a pre-constituted material system. Feenberg's reading thus emphasizes that technology is not a mere neutral instrument applied to previously given ends, but the very crystallization of a social relation in technical form, in which knowledge, initiative and margin of decision are displaced from labor to management and to infrastructure. The conceptual consequence, for the author, is that operational autonomy designates this discretionary capacity to decide and reorganize the process without depending on the point of view and interests of the subordinate actors, precisely because those interests have been downgraded and neutralized at the level of technical organization. <3>↩</3>
“The Internet is a technical system first and foremost. Its social meaning is inextricably intertwined with its technical character.” <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 99)</2>. <3>↩</3>
“I call their goals for the Internet the ‘consumption model’ and the ‘community model,’ respectively.” <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 101)</2>. <3>↩</3>

In Questioning Technology <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 1999, p. 126; 191)</2>, the case of Minitel (Teletel) is presented as a classic example of technical reorientation driven by user agency, that is, of democratic rationalization in operation. The system was conceived and distributed by the French telephone company (France Telecom), which put millions of terminals into circulation free of charge, designed to look like an accessory of the household telephone. This gesture of <3>design</3> and public policy had a relatively clear technocratic direction, that of consolidating an access infrastructure and organizing Minitel as an instrument for the centralized distribution of information and data services. The users' intervention occurs precisely when this design is taken as the starting point for an unforeseen appropriation. The fact that the terminal “disguised itself” as a telephone device suggested to some users that the network could serve for interpersonal communication. From there, users “hacked” the network in which they were inserted and altered its functioning, introducing practices of online human communication, such as anonymous chat, aimed at amusement, companionship and encounters, where the mere distribution of data had been planned. The result is a transformation of the system's social meaning. What had been stabilized as a rationalist medium of information comes to be redefined as a medium of encounter and communication, converting the “cold computer” into a “new hot medium”. The theoretical point is that this trajectory reveals the interpretive flexibility of technology. A set of devices configured to transmit information is perceived by users as a solution for human communication, and this new interpretation ends up pressing for changes and accommodations in the system itself, becoming incorporated into its functioning. The case bears directly on the debate on platforms because it shows, in concrete terms, that purposes are neither the destiny nor the essence of the artifact. They can be disputed in practice, rewritten by uses, and later consolidated by <4>design</4> modifications. This type of reorientation helps explain why “community” and “participation” are not mere social externalities, but dimensions that can shift the very teleology of a network and, later, be reabsorbed into arrangements of governance and monetization. “Users ‘hacked’ the network in which they were inserted and altered its functioning, introducing human communication where only the centralized distribution of information had been planned.” <5>Feenberg</5><6>(Feenberg, 1999, p. 126)</6> <7>↩</7>
“The future of the Internet depends on which actors determine its technical code.” <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 101)</2>. <3>↩</3>
“Many-to-many communication is a typical concretization.” <1>Feenberg</1><2>(Feenberg, 2017, p. 105)</2>. <3>↩</3>

The combined reading of Ellul, Postman, Vanderburg and Feenberg makes it possible to recognize one and the same dynamic from distinct angles. Technical rationality tends to expand as the organizing criterion of everyday life; media ecologies reformat what presents itself as reliable information, acceptable debate and relevant knowledge; and technique incorporated into routines fragments experience, reducing the density of meaning-making and opening space for forms of symbolic steering that do not depend on explicit persuasion. Feenberg completes this picture by preventing the diagnosis from degrading into fatalism: technical rationality is institutionalized in concrete choices, stabilized in design, and therefore remains criticizable, contestable and controllable.

In this scenario, “techno-media order” describes not so much a cultural backdrop as a mode of practical coordination. Systems, interfaces and patterns of circulation come to <1>p. 138</1> organize routines and expectations, defining what appears as possible, probable and desirable. Technique operates as environment, media structure forms of life, and advertising communication, in a broad sense, acts as an engineering of signs that reorders needs, belongings and promises. When these layers combine, ordinary experience no longer depends chiefly on contextual interpretation and comes to be traversed by mediations that anticipate choices, delimit alternatives and rank visibilities.

Digital consumption thus emerges as insertion into continuous operational architectures. The consumer does not merely receive a finished piece of content. They come to inhabit an arrangement of access points, curations, permissions, frictions and update cycles that exists while the system works and while the user remains integrated into it. Experience becomes inseparable from the conditions of its production. The consumed object takes on a relational and architectural form, since it is constituted by mediations that organize enjoyment, permanence, loss, modification and degradation over time.

For this reason, the consumption decision is rarely formed solely by rational comparison of performance, price and suitability. It is also organized by regimes of attention, reputation and belonging, in which value is staged, reiterated and stabilized by presentation formats. Postman explains how rhythm, impact and fragmentation affect credibility and relevance; Vanderburg makes it possible to understand why, in desymbolized routines, goods and services tend to take the place of the recomposition of meaning; and Feenberg offers the material link, by locating practical normativity in design. <1>Defaults</1>, choice hierarchies, recommendation systems, metrics and urgency devices produce an everyday grammar in which certain behaviors are facilitated, others become improbable and many alternatives do not even appear as alternatives.

The vulnerability formed in this environment is not exhausted by lack of information or by classic economic asymmetry. It bears on the capacity to interpret, verify and contest the very field in which choice takes place. The decisive gap now opens between promise and the actual conditions of enjoyment, between sign and delivery, between the performance of belonging and the infrastructure of monetization. Even when there is no textual omission, steering may operate through curation and architecture, before reading and often outside it.

Platforms function as everyday governance. Feenberg describes constraints materialized in systems capable of guiding actions with greater efficacy than political authority, because they bear on reflexes, skills and attitudes, and not only on formal declarations. Normativity ceases to depend solely on explicit commands and comes to operate through architecture. What is permitted, encouraged or punished may be inscribed in interface, flow <1>p. 139</1> and metric, not only in a clause. Terms and notices remain relevant, but cease to be the main place in which power is exercised.

Seen in this key, contracts, private policies, technical standards and property regimes over signs and accesses appear as overlapping layers of one and the same governance. The offer is simultaneously narrative and infrastructure: it mobilizes belonging and recognition while administering visibility, repetition and reward. The question ceases to be only the content of the promise and comes to include the way in which it becomes operative, as well as the mediations that shape enjoyment without allowing themselves to be fully verified by the addressee. This is the conceptual terrain in which the teleology inscribed in design can be reconstructed as a structure of purpose and in which requirements such as auditability and functional value equivalence will come to operate as minimum parameters of legitimacy for exchanges mediated by systems.

Consumption in digital environments does not take place over a neutral medium, nor is it exhausted in contracting for an isolated good or service. The technical-media order designates, here, the regime of technical and communicational mediations that comes to operate as the everyday infrastructure of experience. Interfaces, recommendation systems, metrics, protocols and display formats organize what appears as accessible, desirable, relevant or normal. In this context, the consumption experience tends to stop being a one-off event and comes to take place in ecosystems of continuous mediation, in which enjoyment itself depends on architecture, curation and regimes of signification.

The first layer of this reconstruction starts from Jacques Ellul, whose reading makes it possible to understand the tendency toward autonomization of technical rationality guided by efficiency, predictability and control. Neil Postman shifts the problem to media as a form of life, showing that means of communication alter criteria of relevance, intelligibility <1>p. 86</1> and socially practicable truth. Willem H. Vanderburg adds the critique of desymbolization, making explicit how signs, needs and cultural bonds can be reorganized by advertising and by the technical rationality of consumption. Together, these diagnoses describe an environment in which technique and media cease to operate as external tools and come to constitute structural conditions of everyday life.

Andrew Feenberg's critique prevents this diagnosis from being received as fatalism. If technology is a social construction, concrete mediations matter legally: interfaces, frictions, permissions, incentives and punishments materialize social and economic purposes in artifacts and platforms. The practical normativity of the environment does not derive only from texts, contracts or explicit commands, but from the design and governance choices that organize the field of the possible and the probable. For this reason, technical architecture is not a mere support for the consumer relationship; it is part of the very form by which conduct is guided, expectations are stabilized and losses can be produced.

In this scenario, it becomes possible to understand why, in digital ecosystems, the value of the consumed object is not separated from the mediations that make it enjoyable, accessible and stable over time. Jacques Ellul <1>(1968)</1> describes technique as a system that ceases to operate as a simple instrument and comes to present itself as a reality of its own, no longer limited to being a means, but capable of imposing its logic as an object in itself <2>Ellul</2><3>(Ellul, 1968, p. 65)</3>. This dynamic is guided by efficiency and tends to select automatically the most effective method, so that, once the criterion of efficiency has been measured and established, technique consolidates and expands by its own force <4>Ellul</4><5>(Ellul, 1968, p. 82-83)</5>.

The movement is cumulative and feeds on its own self-growth. Technique reaches a point at which it comes to transform itself and progress with little decisive intervention by man <1>Ellul</1><2>(Ellul, 1968, p. 88-89)</2>. For this reason, its effects go beyond the productive plane and assume a civilizational dimension, insofar as technique expands into all domains, tends to reduce man to the condition of an object and imposes itself as the substance of the social world, and can be described as an entire civilization <3>Ellul</3><4>(Ellul, 1968, p. 5; p. 128)</4>. In this scenario, values and purposes lose centrality because technical rationality operates as a machine of instrumentalization, converting everything into a means and shifting the criterion of decision to the performance of the method and to what works best <5>Ellul</5><6>(Ellul, 1968, p. 145)</6>.

Ellul <1>(1968)</1> insists that the technical phenomenon<2><3>40</3></2> cannot be treated as a particular sector of modernity, because it tends to cut across the very elements of civilization. The <4>p. 87</4> decisive point is that, in whatever domain it is applied, technique presents itself as a rational process, which shifts the social problem into a problem of method <5>Ellul</5><6>(Ellul, 1968, p. 81)</6>. Alternatives come to be filtered by what can be rationalized, measured and operationalized, and the debate on ends tends to be compressed by the grammar of efficiency.

The consequence is a process of standardization and adaptation of the human being to the demands of the technical system, with decision-making power concentrated in bureaucratic structures and substantive margins of self-determination weakened. The effect is a reorganization of modern life in which work, administration and culture come to be shaped by demands of performance, standardization and control, relegating to the background other rationalities (ethical, political and symbolic) that do not translate into efficiency. From this perspective, the technical-media order is neither neutral nor merely instrumental, because it constitutes the practical horizon from which digital experience becomes possible and intelligible and, at the same time, produces the social and cultural conditions that naturalize certain routines, perceptions and consumption behaviors.

Ellul <1>(1968)</1> links the obsession with efficiency and productivity to the production of an inhuman atmosphere, in which work is dehumanized and man distances himself from nature <2>Ellul</2><3>(Ellul, 1968, p. 3)</3>. On the political-economic plane, he maintains that technique favors the formation of an aristocracy of technicians, capable of concentrating knowledge and decisions in opaque circuits that are scarcely accessible to the lay public <4>Ellul</4><5>(Ellul, 1968, p. 165)</5>. When this picture is articulated with the State, democracy is weakened because public debate tends to be replaced by management and by mechanisms of persuasion, with corrosive effects on the citizen's faculty of discernment <6>Ellul</6><7>(Ellul, 1968, p. 281)</7>.

The reference to Ellul matters here as a structural diagnosis of a rationality guided by efficiency, predictability and control, capable of expanding and stabilizing itself as an environment. The analytical gain lies in making visible that, when technique presents itself as “necessity” and as an automatic criterion of decision, purposes and values tend to be compressed by the grammar of what works “best”. This compression is relevant to <1>p. 88</1> digital consumption because in it choices of design and governance are naturalized as if they were mere technical requirements, shifting conflicts outside the field of deliberation and accountability.

It should, however, be made explicit from the outset that drawing on Ellul does not amount here to adherence to technological determinism, but serves as a key to understanding a structural tendency whereby technical rationality, guided by efficiency, predictability and control, tends to spill over specific domains and to reorganize social practices, including consumption. To say that technique acquires “autonomy” does not mean postulating a single, inevitable or monolithic causality, but recognizing that, in certain sociotechnical arrangements, institutional and economic incentives turn innovation and the implementation of systems into a partially self-fueling dynamic, often detached from public deliberation proportional to their effects. It is precisely in this space, between systemic tendency and the possibility of democratic governance, that the legal problem at issue lies. If technical architecture becomes a vector for organizing everyday life, it also becomes a <1>locus</1> of attribution and of assessment of legitimacy, above all when it comes to structure choices, expectations and access regimes that cannot be audited by their addressees or even by legitimate authorities.

Precisely for this reason, the reading of Ellul needs to be articulated with that of Feenberg. The systemic force of technique does not eliminate the fact that artifacts, infrastructures and platforms assume concrete forms through socially situated choices, traversed by interests, disputes and purposes. This passage is decisive for the thesis: if technical architecture organizes the consumption experience, it cannot be treated as nature. It must be read as design, and design is susceptible to critique, control and reorientation.

With Feenberg, the problem shifts from the technical phenomenon in general to specific mediations. Interfaces, frictions, permissions, prohibitions, incentives and punishments are not a simple operational layer; they express a socially situated rationality. In the context of this research, this means that the appearance of inevitability of platforms must also be read as the result of consolidated choices, which come to operate as a naturalized environment. It is this mechanism of naturalization that makes the architecture of platforms legally relevant: it conceals purposes, hinders contestation and shifts conflicts outside the ordinary sphere of accountability.

In continuous digital services, especially in interactive entertainment, the modulation of what can be enjoyed is usually treated by the supplier as an ordinary operation of the system, while the consumer stabilizes expectations of enjoyment and belonging on the basis of <1>p. 89</1> what was promised, acquired and experienced. This gap between regimes of meaning produces qualificatory opacity: it makes it difficult to name the injury, identify the affected object and bring the loss back within the traditional categories of suitability, quality, defect and information. For this reason, architecture and governance must be treated as a material dimension of supply.

The contribution of Neil Postman <1>(2006)</1>, influenced by Ellul<2><3>41</3></2>, shifts the technical diagnosis to the plane of media as the dominant cultural form. In <4>Amusing Ourselves to Death</4>, the author analyzes how television, by replacing the printed word as the main means of public communication, reorganizes the form of discourse and, with it, reconfigures cultural content itself. Politics, religion and education come to operate under the grammar of entertainment, in a society that approaches the condition of “amusing ourselves to death” <5>Postman</5><6>(Postman, 2006, [p. 16])</6>.

In the political field, visual logic shifts the weight of argument to appearance, performance and impression management, reducing the centrality of programs, ideologies and substantive confrontations of ideas <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 16])</2>. In the religious domain, television tends to convert the experience of transcendence into spectacle, emptying ritual density and symbolic depth <3>Postman</3><4>(Postman, 2006, [p. 79])</4>. In education, a pedagogical philosophy guided by immediate accessibility and contentment is consolidated, to the detriment of cognitive effort and more demanding intellectual formation <5>Postman</5><6>(Postman, 2006, [p. 96])</6>. The common point is the reconfiguration of the social criteria of attention, relevance and truth.

In the contemporary digital environment, this contribution gains additional specificity. The epistemological reconfiguration no longer stems only from the predominance of image or entertainment, but from the passage to interactive, personalized and metrified ecosystems, in which the circulation of statements is modulated by recommendation, ranking and differential distribution of visibility. If on television entertainment colonizes public discourse through a relatively uniform schedule, on platforms it is coupled to the capture of attention based on continuous <1>feedback</1>, permanent testing and interface micro-optimizations. This shift is decisive for the thesis because the problem is no longer only the superficialization of content, but the production of a regime of reality in which signs, promises and <2>p. 90</2> performances of belonging guide consumer conduct and form part of the semiotic materiality of the IOC.

Drawing on Feenberg, this epistemological reconfiguration can also be read as politics built into technical design. Personalization, ranking and metrification are not mere functionalities, since they materialize criteria of value and visibility that guide behavior at scale. The passage from television to platforms, therefore, is not a simple change of medium, but a change of architecture: entertainment and attention become operationalizable by technical structures that organize the field of the possible and the probable. For the IOC, this means that the offer cannot be reduced to the final content, since it includes the designed mediations that make this content consumable and carry identifiable teleologies, even if they are not openly presented.

The work of Willem H. Vanderburg <1>(2011)</1> deepens this critique by examining advertising as an interested catalyst of cultural desymbolization<2><3>42</3></2>, the process by which artificial needs are produced and excessive consumption is normalized. For the author, companies mobilize cultural symbols to attribute to material products the illusory capacity to satisfy emotional and social needs, which is particularly serious when this dynamic targets children, who are less able to distinguish programming from advertising. Advertising, in this framework, manipulates vulnerabilities, weakens cultural symbols and demands constant strategic reinvention to remain effective.

Vanderburg also problematizes the absence of substantive information in advertisements, whose aim is no longer to inform but to steer consumer conduct. From a transnational perspective, he points to obstacles to the democratic regulation of excessive advertising, especially when corporate rights prevail over the rights of communities. Advertising does not merely shape individual behavior; it perpetuates a cycle of consumption harmful to social well-being and establishes itself as a significant tool of the technical order.

<1>p. 91</1> In digital ecosystems, Vanderburg's critique of advertising gains new reach: desymbolization does not act only in advertising discourse, but is coupled to technical architectures that administer visibility, repetition and reward. With Feenberg <2>(2017)</2>, the advertisement ceases to be a separate event and becomes a component of a designed environment, in which the circulation of signs is programmed to produce need, adherence and permanence. Semiotic manipulation, therefore, does not occur only through the content of messages, but through the form of their distribution and through the interface logic that defines when, how and for whom certain signs appear. This intensifies the problem of auditability and shifts the debate from persuasion to the governance of the field of experience.

The mention of transnational arenas, such as international trade, does not function here as a conclusive statement about a specific body, but as an indication of a structural problem: the delocalization and multilevel complexification of the conditions for regulating advertising and consumption in digital ecosystems. The desymbolization described by Vanderburg matters because it reveals a pattern of governance of consumption through signs that often exceeds the addressee's horizon of control and, not infrequently, also the immediate reach of traditional regulatory responses.

On platforms, this semiotic governance is reinforced by contracts, private moderation policies and proprietary infrastructures for the circulation of content. In this layer, intellectual property rights appear not only as protection of creations, but as a legal technology for the control of signs, the delimitation of uses and the stabilization of expectations of enjoyment. The point is not to shift the axis to a macroinstitutional debate, but to make visible that contemporary semiotic manipulation operates in ecosystems in which normative and technical layers overlap, aggravating the asymmetry between those who design and those who consume.

The characterization of digital consumption as mediated and continued enjoyment finds support in Brazilian positive law, which already recognizes, in specific disciplines linked to software and related services, duties of functional continuity and technical support tied to the economic exploitation of the object. For the purposes of this section, the reference does not anticipate the later dogmatic construction; it only shows that dependence on maintenance, updating and governance over time is not an accident external to the consumer relationship, but an attributable feature of supply in digital environments.

In this environment, consumer vulnerability tends to manifest itself as the distance between the promised, curated and displayed experience and the actual conditions of enjoyment, modification, continuity and loss. Protection concerning suitability, quality, defect and information comes to depend <1>p. 92</1> on the possibility of auditing and controlling mediations that organize the field of the possible and the probable. For this reason, before formulating the legal regime of the IOC, it is necessary to understand how technique becomes autonomous, how media reorganize the intelligibility of consumption and how design transforms economic choices into an everyday environment.

For Jacques Ellul <1>(1968)</1>, “technique” is not equivalent to machines, nor to the mechanical apparatus taken in isolation: “Whoever says technique immediately thinks of machine”, but this identification is a recurring error <2>Ellul</2><3>(Ellul, 1968, p. 1)</3>. This is because technique “has now assumed almost complete autonomy in relation to the machine”, surpassing the status of a simple instrument and coming to operate as a phenomenon of its own <4>Ellul</4><5>(Ellul, 1968, p. 2)</5>. In this key, technique presents itself as rationalization guided by efficiency, insofar as the “satisfactory” and “efficient” method tends to impose itself by itself — the “the one best way” mentioned earlier — and, with this, the technical decision comes to have the form of an objective necessity: “there is no choice between two technical methods: one imposes itself fatally because its results are counted, measured, patent and indisputable” <6>Ellul</6><7>(Ellul, 1968, p. 83)</7>. By penetrating “into all domains and into man himself” and tending to encompass the maximum of domains in order to be effective, technique ceases to be merely an object for man and “becomes his very substance”, acquiring totalizing reach <8>Ellul</8><9>(Ellul, 1968, p. 5)</9>. In this generalization, its performance criteria are converted into a practical measure of social decision, and the autonomy of the technical system restricts the possibility of human deliberation on ends: “the autonomy of technique therefore prevents man, at present, from choosing his destiny” <10>Ellul</10><11>(Ellul, 1968, p. 143)</11>. <12>↩</12>

Influenced by the work of Jacques Ellul, Postman treats technology not as a neutral tool, but as a rationality that tends to impose itself on institutions and culture through criteria of efficiency, standardization and control. On this basis, he shifts the diagnosis to media and education and maintains that media and their technical forms reorganize what counts as truth, relevance and attention, with effects of impoverishment of public debate and reduction of symbolic experience. In this framing, the critique is not an aversion to technology itself, but the defense of limits and of human criteria of judgment, such as purpose, meaning and responsibility, when technical rationality comes to operate as the dominant parameter. <1>↩</1>

According to Willem H. Vanderburg <1>(2016)</1>, cultural desymbolization is the process by which the human capacity to attribute meaning to experiences is weakened, resulting in a fragmented and impoverished understanding of life as a whole. The process occurs when social, cultural and physical constraints limit people's participation, freedom and commitment, forcing them to navigate a fragmented world dominated by narrow, one-off objectives and by technological connectivity. Although desymbolization is not a new phenomenon, Vanderburg argues that, in modern societies, it takes on graver dimensions owing to the growing separation between knowledge and experience, fostering a dichotomy between "reality" and a "symbolically reduced universe." Desymbolization profoundly affects the way people experience the world, which he represents through an analogy with "mental maps". In traditional societies, these maps are densely connected, offering a rich network of meanings. In modern societies, however, as desymbolization intensifies, these maps become simplified, reducing symbolic connections and the capacity to understand life in its complexity. For Vanderburg, this process, exacerbated by reliance on disciplinary approaches disconnected from culture, results in a disjointed and divided world. <2>↩</2>
